prize_parts.citation: For the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: Pd-catalysed C-N coupling is the clearest case on the shortlist of a general method that changed how chemists everywhere build bonds. Aryl amines went from a forcing, narrow transformation to a routine one through ligand-controlled oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination. The evidence is in adoption: it is used daily in pharmaceutical and materials synthesis and appears in countless total syntheses. Thirty years of independent confirmation and a stable mechanistic picture mean there is no maturity risk. Buchwald and Hartwig independently established the general catalytic method in 1994-1995 and then drove ligand design, so a two-person prize with a clean citation is attributable. It is also the only core molecule-making achievement on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The 2010 prize for Pd-catalysed cross-coupling (Heck, Negishi, Suzuki) will make some colleagues see C-N coupling as an extension of a recognised field rather than a new principle, and Brzezinski's novelty worry is fair. Kosugi's tin-amide precedent is a genuine antecedent whose weight I have not independently verified. The candidate also has the thinnest opening support on the shortlist, with only two members ranking it, so it may simply not command a majority.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks targeted protein degradation first because removing a protein rather than blocking it is a new pharmacological principle with real consequences and molecules in the clinic, while noting that clinical validation is still maturing and that credit is crowded.
responses.response: I agree the principle is new and the clinical pipeline is real, which is why I rank B011 seventh rather than low and keep it as an alternative. My reservation is about what was new chemically. The design rules are a medicinal chemistry achievement, but the concept came from cell biology, and with no approved degrader the impact is promised rather than demonstrated. The credit problem is also real: Sakamoto, Kim, Handa, Ito and Gray are all excluded by a Crews-Deshaies-Ciulli trio. I would not block B011 if the committee converges on it, but I do not accept that it is clearly ahead of a method whose impact we can already count in syntheses.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks C-N coupling fifth, calling it transformative and mature but noting that cross-coupling already received the 2010 prize, and asks whether Kosugi should be included.
responses.response: The 2010 overlap is the strongest objection, and I would answer it on chemical grounds. The 2010 prize concerned C-C bond formation from organometallic partners. C-N coupling needed a different mechanistic solution, since amine binding, deprotonation and C-N reductive elimination had to be tamed with new ligand classes, and that is why it came two decades later. On Kosugi, I would keep the prize at two: his stannyl-amide reaction was a precursor that was not general and not catalytic in amine. I accept that this is a judgement call and that the committee could reasonably credit him.

responses.point: Aili ranks degraders first as a new modality, and ranks genetic code expansion (B042) fourth, calling it broadly impactful and mature, with Schultz as founder and Chin and Wang as extenders.
responses.response: I take the genetic code expansion point more seriously than my opening ballot suggested. It is mature and chemically inventive, in that orthogonal pairs give chemists direct control over protein composition, so I list B042 as an alternative. My hesitation is that the invention is largely a biological engineering of the translation machinery, and the Schultz, Chin, Wang split is not settled. If the committee wants a chemical biology prize this year, I find B042 easier to defend than B011 on both maturity and attribution.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sequencing first and Gratzel-O'Regan solar cells second, favouring ideas that moved from physical principle to deployed tool, and ranks B011 third.
responses.response: I share the criterion that a clear principle must become a tool others use, and I think B055 meets it more fully than nanopores, whose attribution you yourself call contested because Branton and Kasianowicz are left out. On the Gratzel-O'Regan cell, the principle is clean and I do not dispute its originality. My question is whether the practical impact justifies the prize, since efficiencies have plateaued and commercial uptake is modest. I would rank it above B011 only if the committee puts a high value on the later perovskite lineage.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats C-N coupling as distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize.
Whether Kosugi's tin-amide work should be credited, and whether the two-person choice survives scrutiny of priority.
Whether B011 attracts a majority despite crowded credit and no approved degrader, in which case I would need to decide how hard to hold my first choice.
I have not independently verified priority details or current clinical status for any candidate.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: none of the credited names for B055 is a mentor, collaborator or institutional colleague. My Masamune background is in stereocontrolled synthesis, not in coupling catalysis. My professional proximity to synthetic methodology is a perspective bias that colleagues should weigh, not a recusal issue.
